title: Cash Transfer Programs in India: An Analytical Study of Structure, Modalities, and Reach
content: This article examines the structure, modalities, and reach of Cash Transfer (CT) and Direct Benefit Transfer programs in India, highlighting their role in poverty alleviation and fulfilling the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Using a qualitative framework, the study synthesises data from central and state government policy documents, official portals, and peer-reviewed literature to establish a systematic typology and comparative analysis of existing schemes. At the national level, centrally sponsored schemes employ digital payment channels and Aadhaar-linked verification to deliver substantial financial aid across multiple sectors. For FY 2024–25, total central cash transfers reached ₹6,89,708 crore across 9.31 billion transactions. Major allocations go to food distribution and fertiliser subsidies, as well as key initiatives such as MGNREGS, PAHAL, PM-KISAN, and PMAY-G. In addition to central measures, state governments implement unconditional and conditional cash transfers to address regional needs. State-level interventions primarily focus on women's empowerment through universal basic income models, input support for farmers, and targeted incentives to reduce female dropout rates and child marriage. Although CTs have improved benefit delivery and reduced leakages, challenges like payment delays, exclusionary targeting criteria, and funding constraints remain. This analysis highlights the necessity for context-specific evaluations to optimise welfare allocation and implementation.
